days.title: Homeostasis — Steady Internal Conditions
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define homeostasis.
  • Explain why organisms need stable internal conditions.
  • Identify examples of homeostasis in plants and animals.
  • Describe the roles of various organ systems in maintaining homeostasis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Homeostasis — maintenance of a stable internal environment.
  • Set point — the target value a system tries to maintain.
  • Sensor — detects changes.
  • Effector — produces the response.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Why Homeostasis Matters

Enzymes and cells work best under specific conditions (temperature, pH, ion concentrations). Without homeostasis, proteins denature and life processes fail.

B. Homeostatic Variables

VariableNormal Range
Body temperature (human)~36.5–37.5 °C
Blood pH~7.35–7.45
Blood glucose~70–110 mg/dL (fasting)
Osmotic balance~0.9% NaCl

C. Examples in Organisms

  • Animals: sweating, shivering, insulin/glucagon, kidney filtration
  • Plants: stomatal control, water uptake by roots, turgor regulation

scenarios.text: Body temperature rises during exercise.
Blood pH is normally 7.4.
Sweat glands produce sweat.
A plant closes stomata in drought.
Kidneys filter blood and adjust water.
Insulin lowers blood glucose.

choices.label: Maintenance of a stable internal environment

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an example of homeostasis?

choices.label: To keep enzymes and cells working optimally

takeaways: Set points, sensors, and effectors maintain balance.
Enzymes work best under specific conditions.
Plants and animals both regulate homeostasis.

days.title: Negative Feedback Loops
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define negative feedback.
  • Identify components of a feedback loop.
  • Describe examples of negative feedback.
  • Explain how negative feedback maintains homeostasis.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Negative feedback — response reverses the original stimulus.
  • Stimulus — change that triggers the loop.
  • Response — action that counteracts the stimulus.
  • Receptor, control center, effector — the three parts.

📚 Lesson Content

A. How Negative Feedback Works

  1. Stimulus — a change from the set point
  2. Receptor — detects the change
  3. Control center — processes the info
  4. Effector — produces a response
  5. Response — reverses the change

B. Examples

SystemStimulusResponse
ThermoregulationBody too hotSweating, vasodilation
ThermoregulationBody too coldShivering, vasoconstriction
Blood glucoseHigh glucoseInsulin released
Blood glucoseLow glucoseGlucagon released
OsmoregulationDehydrationADH released → water reabsorbed

scenarios.text: Body temperature rises → sweating begins.
Blood glucose is high → insulin released.
Blood glucose is low → glucagon released.
Body temperature drops → shivering.
A person is dehydrated → ADH released.
Blood calcium drops → PTH released.

questions.text: In negative feedback, the response does what to the stimulus?
Which hormone is released when blood glucose is HIGH?
Sweating when hot is an example of:

takeaways: It consists of a stimulus, receptor, control center, effector, and response.
Most homeostatic mechanisms are negative feedback loops.

days.title: Positive Feedback Loops
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define positive feedback.
  • Differentiate positive from negative feedback.
  • Describe examples of positive feedback.
  • Explain why positive feedback must be short-lived.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Positive feedback — response amplifies the original stimulus.
  • Amplification — increases the stimulus.
  • Stop signal — external event that halts the loop.

📚 Lesson Content

A. How Positive Feedback Works

The response increases the original stimulus, causing further response. This cycle continues until an external event stops it.

B. Examples

SystemStimulusResponseStop
ChildbirthPressure on cervixOxytocin → more contractionsBaby delivered
Blood clottingVessel injuryPlatelets attract more plateletsClot formed
LactationSucklingProlactin → more milkStop nursing

C. Why It Must Stop

Runaway positive feedback is dangerous — e.g., uncontrolled clotting or runaway fever.

scenarios.text: Uterine contractions strengthen until baby is born.
Platelets release chemicals that attract more platelets.
Sweating to cool down.
Oxytocin release during labor.
Insulin lowers blood sugar.
Milk production increases with nursing.

questions.text: In positive feedback, the response does what to the stimulus?
Which of the following is a positive feedback loop?

takeaways: It must be stopped by an external event.
Runaway positive feedback can be dangerous.

days.title: Real-Life Homeostasis Examples
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Apply homeostasis concepts to real-life scenarios.
  • Describe plant homeostasis mechanisms.
  • Describe animal homeostasis mechanisms.
  • Analyze what happens when homeostasis fails.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Thermoregulation — temperature balance.
  • Osmoregulation — water/salt balance.
  • Glucoregulation — glucose balance.
  • Homeostatic failure — disease or death.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Animal Homeostasis

  • Temperature: sweating, shivering, vasodilation, vasoconstriction
  • Glucose: insulin, glucagon
  • Water: ADH, kidneys
  • pH: buffers, breathing rate

B. Plant Homeostasis

  • Water: stomatal opening/closing via guard cells
  • Temperature: transpiration cooling
  • Nutrients: root uptake, vascular transport
  • Turgor: vacuole regulation

C. When Homeostasis Fails

FailureResult
Thermoregulation fails (high)Heat stroke
Thermoregulation fails (low)Hypothermia
Glucose regulation failsDiabetes
Osmoregulation failsDehydration or edema

scenarios.text: A person exercises in hot weather.
A person walks in the cold.
A plant wilts.
A person eats a large meal.
A person hasn't drunk water all day.
A marathon runner collapses with heat stroke.

questions.text: Which is a plant homeostatic mechanism?
What happens when thermoregulation fails in hot weather?

takeaways: Homeostasis maintains temperature, water, glucose, and pH.
Plants regulate water via stomata; animals via kidneys and hormones.
Real-life examples: sweating, shivering, insulin, ADH.
